title: Modifiers and parallel structure
note: Put a modifier next to the word it describes. A misplaced modifier sits too far from its word; a dangling modifier has no word in the sentence to describe, so an opening phrase must refer to the subject that follows it. Parallel structure puts paired or listed ideas in the same grammatical form.

read.title: Who is doing the walking?
text: Readers assume that a modifier describes the nearest word it could sensibly describe. When that assumption fails, sentences turn strange. "Walking to class, the rain soaked my notes" says that the rain was walking. The opening phrase walking to class wants a person, but the subject that follows is rain. This is a dangling modifier: the word it should describe never appears.
The fix is to put the walker in the subject slot: "Walking to class, I got my notes soaked in the rain." Or turn the phrase into a full clause: "As I walked to class, the rain soaked my notes."

A misplaced modifier is a different problem. Its word is present but too far away. "She served pizza to the guests on paper plates" seats the guests on the plates. Move the phrase: "She served the guests pizza on paper plates." Small words such as only, almost and just are the most often misplaced. "He almost failed every test" and "He failed almost every test" report very different semesters.
When you revise, look at each opening phrase and ask whether the subject right after the comma is the one doing that action.

q.q: What is wrong with "Walking to class, the rain soaked my notes"?
o: It says the rain was walking
The verb disagrees with its subject

q.q: How does a misplaced modifier differ from a dangling one?
o: Its word is present but too far away

q.q: "He failed almost every test" means that he...
o: came close to failing each test
